summary: This work analyzes fault-tolerant logical operations in modular quantum architectures by simulating distributed CNOT gates via lattice surgery between noisy QPUs connected by imperfect Bell pairs, and develops efficient protocols for preparing distributed logical GHZ states. The key finding is that interfaces tolerate noise up to $\alpha = 20$ times higher than intra-QPU noise (threshold degradation only $2$–$3 \times 10^{-3}$), and ancilla minimization for GHZ state preparation reduces to a polynomial-time vertex-cover problem on spanning trees.
motivation: Modular quantum computing requires understanding how errors at module interfaces affect fault-tolerant computation beyond logical-memory benchmarks. Prior distributed QEC studies focused on state preservation; this work addresses circuit-level performance of nonlocal logical entangling gates, which are essential for scalable distributed quantum computing.
method: Circuit-level simulations using LOOM and STIM with depolarizing noise model ($p_g = \epsilon$ local, $p_g = \alpha \epsilon$ nonlocal) and PyMatching decoding, studying three bipartite and tripartite CNOT configurations. GHZ preparation uses iterative local-state fusion via nonlocal CNOT, formulated as graph optimization: minimum vertex cover on spanning trees with BFS/DFS/Star-Search heuristics.
result: Distributed CNOT thresholds remain near monolithic baseline ($\approx 10^{-3}$) despite $\alpha=20$ interface noise penalty. For $n$-QPU networks: minimum ancilla QPUs equal maximum matching of optimal spanning tree; Bell-pair consumption fixed at $d(2d-1)(n-1)$; fusion depth trades between $O(\log n)$ (high ancilla) and $O(n)$ (minimal ancilla); Star-Search heuristic outperforms BFS/DFS in reducing ancilla requirements by $\sim 15$–$30\%$ on random graphs.
